winterswijk.intro: The oldest tree in Winterswijk, by the reckoning of the local history society, is an oak in a pasture at Brinkheurne, planted between 1750 and 1800. Lightning tore its bark open in 1975; it was repaired in 1981 and has kept growing, to 6 metres round by 2015. It stands alone in the field because the hedge bank it grew in was cleared in the 19th century and this tree was left.
winterswijk.meta_description: The old oak of Sieverdink near Winterswijk: about 250 years old, 6 metres round, struck by lightning in 1975 and still growing.
winterswijk.question_answer: The oldest tree in Winterswijk is the Oude eik van Sieverdink, a pedunculate oak in a pasture at Brinkheurne, according to the local history society Oud-Winterswijk. The national register's claim form dates its planting to between 1750 and 1800, so it is roughly 250 years old. In 2015 it measured 6 metres round and 20 metres tall. It survived a lightning strike in September 1975 that tore away its bark over many metres.
winterswijk.question_meta: Winterswijk's oldest tree is the Sieverdink oak at Brinkheurne, planted between 1750 and 1800 and 6 metres round in 2015.
winterswijk.question_context: The Sieverdink oak stands in the countryside of Winterswijk, in the hamlet of Brinkheurne, by a farm of the same name on Bothoekweg. Dutch Wikipedia notes that it may in fact stand just across the line in the neighbouring hamlet of Kotten. The tree began as part of a houtwal, a wooded hedge bank, and when the bank was cleared in the 19th century the oak was the one left standing. That is why it now has a pasture to itself. Its girth grew from 5 metres in 1972 to 6 metres in 2015, lightning and tree surgery included. In 2018 a group of 24 photographers made it the subject of an exhibition and a book. The meadow is private farmland and no source says it may be entered, so the view is from the public roads, Sieverdinkweg and Bothoekweg, which meet just to the northeast. No bus time has been confirmed; it is a walk or a bicycle ride out from Winterswijk. Our pin is close to the tree rather than exact.

faq.q: How old is the oldest tree in Winterswijk?
faq.a: Roughly 250 years. The register's claim form puts the planting of the Sieverdink oak between 1750 and 1800.

faq.q: Can you walk up to the Sieverdink oak?
faq.a: No source says the pasture may be entered. It is working farmland, so look at the tree from Sieverdinkweg or Bothoekweg.

faq.q: What happened to the oak in 1975?
faq.a: Lightning struck it in September 1975, tearing off bark over many metres and breaking branches. Tree surgeons repaired it in 1981, and it has added about 80 centimetres of girth since the strike.

leonstein.intro: Leonstein's best-known tree has its own parking bay and bench. The Bühler-Linde is a very large, multi-stemmed large-leaved lime on the grass at a road junction, in front of the Hasengütl farm that locals also call Bühler. Its age has never been published, and its story lives mostly in one photographer's record, which makes it a tree to see for yourself.
leonstein.meta_description: The Bühler-Linde in Leonstein, Upper Austria: a huge multi-stemmed lime at a road junction, with its own parking bay and bench.
leonstein.question_answer: The Bühler-Linde is a very large, multi-stemmed large-leaved lime standing in front of the Hasengütl farm in Leonstein, part of Grünburg in Upper Austria. It has a signposted parking bay and a bench beside it at the road junction. Its age, girth and height have not been published, and it is not on Upper Austria's list of natural monuments.
leonstein.question_meta: The Bühler-Linde: a vast multi-stemmed lime in front of the Hasengütl farm in Leonstein, Upper Austria, with a bench and parking bay.
leonstein.question_context: Leonstein is a village in the municipality of Grünburg, in Upper Austria. The lime grows at a road junction in front of the Hasengütl farm, Heindlmühlstraße 1, a farm that also goes by the names Bühler and Höchtl; the tree takes the first of them. Someone thought it worth a signposted parking bay and a bench, though it is not even on the list of protected trees. Photographs from May 2021 and March 2022 show a broad crown on several stems, with mistletoe hanging in it. The species, a large-leaved lime, flowers in June, a little earlier than other limes, with pale scented blossom that draws bees for about a fortnight; that is the time to come. The farm is private. The tree stands on the grass by the road, so everything worth seeing is visible from the junction and the bench. No public-transport time to the village has been checked. Nobody has published how old the tree is. If you know, or know who planted it, we would like to hear.

faq.q: Is the Bühler-Linde a protected natural monument?
faq.a: Not as far as we can find. It does not appear on Upper Austria's list of natural monuments.

faq.q: When does the Bühler-Linde flower?
faq.a: Large-leaved limes flower in June, for about a fortnight, with pale and scented blossom.

faq.q: Can you park near the tree?
faq.a: Yes. There is a signposted parking bay and a bench beside the road at the junction. The farm itself is private.

hochosterwitz.intro: Below Hochosterwitz castle, at the south foot of its hill, stands a lime with its age written on a plaque on its own trunk: about 450 years. That plaque is the only record we have found. The trunk is massive, with big buttress roots under a crown of upright limbs, and a wooden bench sits beside it on the open wooded slope. The castle up the hill charges for entry; the tree does not.
hochosterwitz.meta_description: A lime at the foot of Hochosterwitz castle hill in Carinthia, about 450 years old by the plaque on its trunk, with a bench beside it.
hochosterwitz.question_answer: At the south foot of the Hochosterwitz castle hill, near Maigern in Carinthia, stands a lime whose plaque gives its age as about 450 years. That figure comes from the plaque alone; the tree is not on Carinthia's list of natural monuments and no survey has measured it. It has a massive trunk with buttress roots and a candelabra crown.
hochosterwitz.question_meta: The lime below Hochosterwitz castle, Carinthia: about 450 years old according to the plaque on its trunk, at the foot of the castle hill.
hochosterwitz.question_context: Hochosterwitz castle crowns a hill near Maigern in Carinthia, and the castle charges for entry. The lime does not. It grows at the south foot of the hill, a few hundred metres below the castle, on an open wooded slope with no fence or gate in sight, and a wooden bench stands next to it. A small plaque on the trunk reads "Linde, Alter etwa 450 Jahre", lime, about 450 years old, and that is the whole of its written record. The photographs we know of were taken in December 2019, when the tree was bare, so they show the shape well: a huge trunk flaring into buttress roots, upright limbs branching like a candelabra, and mistletoe in the crown. They do not show the leaves, which is why nobody has yet recorded which kind of lime it is. A visit in summer would settle that, and a dated photograph would confirm that it still stands, since we have found nothing newer than 2019. No public-transport time has been checked. Our pin comes from a GPS fix at the tree.

faq.q: How old is the lime at Hochosterwitz?
faq.a: About 450 years, according to the plaque on its trunk. We have found no other source for the figure.

faq.q: Do you need a castle ticket to see the tree?
faq.a: No. The lime stands at the foot of the hill, on open slope below the castle, which charges for entry further up.

faq.q: What kind of lime is it?
faq.a: That is not recorded. The only photographs were taken in winter, without leaves. If you photograph its leaves in summer, tell us.

bregenz.intro: Bregenz protects a Japanese pagoda tree in Rieden-Vorkloster that is remarkable less for its age than for its shape: a crown 26 metres wide on a tree only 12.5 metres tall. Planted around 1950, it became a natural monument in July 2010 and stands beside a school on Johann-Jörg-Weg, seen from the street. Come in August, when the species opens its cream flowers and little else in town is in bloom.
bregenz.meta_description: A Japanese pagoda tree in Bregenz with a crown 26 metres wide on a 12.5 metre tree, a natural monument since 2010, flowering in August.
bregenz.question_answer: The Japanese pagoda tree on Johann-Jörg-Weg in Bregenz's Rieden-Vorkloster district is a natural monument, declared by the town council on 1 July 2010 and listed in the Vorarlberg register as ND-213. Planted around 1950, it is about 75 years old, 12.5 metres tall, with a trunk 86 centimetres thick and a crown 26 metres across.
bregenz.question_meta: Bregenz's Japanese pagoda tree on Johann-Jörg-Weg: a natural monument since 2010, 12.5 metres tall with a 26 metre crown.
bregenz.question_context: Rieden-Vorkloster is a district of Bregenz, the capital of Vorarlberg on Lake Constance. The pagoda tree grows at the edge of the schoolyard of the district's Hauptschule, with its trunk right at the street behind a low hedge, so the street is where you stand to see it. The school grounds are not open to visitors. It is a young tree by the standards of this map, planted around 1950. What sets it apart is proportion. Its crown, at 26 metres, is more than twice as wide as the tree is tall, and in July 2010 the town council made it a natural monument. A newspaper report that year called it vital, with 11 to 25 percent leaf loss. The species flowers late, in August, with clusters of cream blossom at a time when little else is in flower, and that is the month to come. The most recent photograph we know of was taken in May 2016, in full leaf, and we have found no newer report on its health. Our pin is approximate; look for the hedge on Johann-Jörg-Weg.

faq.q: Why is the pagoda tree in Bregenz a natural monument?
faq.a: For its crown, 26 metres wide on a tree 12.5 metres tall. The town council declared it a natural monument on 1 July 2010.

faq.q: When does the Bregenz pagoda tree flower?
faq.a: In August. Japanese pagoda trees open cream flowers in late summer, when little else is in bloom.

faq.q: Can you enter the school grounds to see it?
faq.a: No. The trunk stands at the edge of Johann-Jörg-Weg behind a low hedge, so see it from the street.

ogi.intro: In Ogi Park, in Saga Prefecture, a Buddhist pine has been clipped into a cube for generations. It is called the kaku-maki, the squared maki, and local tradition puts it at about 350 years old, a figure no survey has checked. It holds no natural monument status, yet visitor information for the park still names it among the things to see. The park is public, open all year, and free as far as any source mentions.
ogi.meta_description: The kaku-maki of Ogi Park, Saga: a Buddhist pine clipped into a cube for generations, about 350 years old by local tradition.
ogi.question_answer: The kaku-maki in Ogi Park, Saga Prefecture, is a Buddhist pine (inumaki) pruned by generations of gardeners into the shape of a cube; kaku-maki means squared maki. Local tradition gives its age as about 350 years, with published figures between 300 and 350. It is not a designated natural monument, but current visitor information for the park still names it among the things to see.
ogi.question_meta: Ogi Park's kaku-maki is a Buddhist pine clipped into a cube, about 300 to 350 years old by local tradition, in Saga Prefecture.
ogi.question_context: Ogi Park is in the town of Ogi, in Saga Prefecture on the island of Kyushu, and it counts among Japan's 100 notable historic parks. The kaku-maki grows inside the park. Its fame is not size but discipline: a crown that has been cut square by one gardener after another, for generations. The age of about 350 years is tradition rather than measurement, and we have found no survey behind it, so treat it as the park's story about itself. A photograph from December 2017 shows the tree in place, and visitor information gathered up to January 2026 still lists the 350-year-old kakumaki as a feature. The park is open all year and no source mentions a ticket. Being an evergreen, the tree looks much the same in every season, so there is no best month for it, only the park's own seasons around it. Our pin comes from where a photographer stood, so it is close rather than exact; once inside the park, the square crown is easy to pick out. No train or bus time from Saga has been checked.

faq.q: What does kaku-maki mean?
faq.a: Squared maki. The maki is an inumaki, a Buddhist pine, and the kaku is the cube its crown has been clipped into.

faq.q: How old is the kaku-maki in Ogi Park?
faq.a: About 350 years by local tradition, with published figures from 300 to 350. We have found no survey that measured it.

faq.q: Is there an entry fee for Ogi Park?
faq.a: No source we have seen mentions one. The park is public and open all year.

hagerum.intro: Just west of the Hägerum manor farm in Oskarshamn municipality grows an oak that measured 6.95 metres round at chest height in 2003, a richly branched tree with a broad crown. It has been a protected natural monument since 1958, though nobody has recorded its age or even which oak it is. It stands in a fenced pasture beside a farm track, and the view is from the path outside the fence.
hagerum.meta_description: Hägerums ek near Oskarshamn: an oak 6.95 metres round, a protected natural monument since 1958, beside a farm track at Hägerum.
hagerum.question_answer: Hägerums ek is an oak just west of the Hägerum manor farm in Döderhult parish, Oskarshamn municipality, Kalmar county. It was protected as a naturminne on 22 August 1958, and in 2003 the Biological Museum in Oskarshamn measured its girth at 6.95 metres at breast height. It is described as richly branched with a broad crown. Its age is not recorded.
hagerum.question_meta: Hägerums ek, near Oskarshamn in Kalmar county: an oak 6.95 metres round and a protected natural monument since 22 August 1958.
hagerum.question_context: Hägerum is a manor farm in Döderhult parish, in Oskarshamn municipality on the Småland coast of Kalmar county. The oak stands just west of the farm buildings, in a fenced pasture beside a farm track. A photograph from 2019 shows a visitor on the path outside the fence, and that is as close as any source takes you: none describes a right of way into the field, so the fence is the edge of the visit and the farm is to be left alone. The Biological Museum in Oskarshamn measured its girth at 6.95 metres in 2003 and describes it as richly branched with a broad crown. The county protected it in 1958. Photographs from May and June 2019 are the most recent sign of it we have found. Neither its age nor its exact species has been written down; it is probably a pedunculate oak, but no source confirms that. No public-transport time from Oskarshamn has been checked, so plan on a car or bicycle.

faq.q: Can you visit Hägerums ek?
faq.a: You can see it from the path outside the fence of the pasture where it grows. No source describes a right of way into the field, so stay outside the fence.

faq.q: How big is Hägerums ek?
faq.a: It measured 6.95 metres round at breast height in 2003, according to the Biological Museum in Oskarshamn.

faq.q: How old is the oak at Hägerum?
faq.a: No source gives an age. It has been a protected natural monument since 1958.

shikokuchuo.intro: Shikokuchuo, in Ehime, has two very different giants. In the town at Shimokashiwa, a Chinese juniper more than 8 metres round has been a National Natural Monument since 1924 and now leans on many wooden props. High on Mt Tamatori, a katsura has lost its central trunk and grown into a ring of stems 15 metres round and 30 metres tall.
shikokuchuo.meta_description: Shikokuchuo's two giants: a juniper 8 metres round, a National Natural Monument since 1924, and a 30 metre katsura on Mt Tamatori.
shikokuchuo.question_answer: Shikokuchuo in Ehime Prefecture has two famous old trees. The Shimokashiwa juniper is a Chinese juniper designated a National Natural Monument in December 1924, measured then at about 8.2 metres round below a large burl. The great katsura of Mt Tamatori is an Ehime Prefecture Natural Monument, more than 300 years old, 30 metres tall and 15 metres round, a ring of stems around a hollow base.
shikokuchuo.question_meta: Shikokuchuo's old trees: the Shimokashiwa juniper, a National Natural Monument since 1924, and the 30 metre katsura on Mt Tamatori.
shikokuchuo.question_context: Shikokuchuo lies on the north side of Shikoku, in Ehime Prefecture, and its two famous trees could hardly be further apart in what a visit asks of you. The juniper is the easy one. It stands on a small plot beside the road in Shimokashiwa, propped on many poles with a stone marker at its foot, and you see it from the roadside; directions point to a drive along National Route 11. One account says a Jizo statue has sat in a hollow at its base since 1783. The katsura is the hard one. It grows at about 1,060 metres on the north slope of Mt Tamatori in the Tomisato district, roughly 25 kilometres of mountain road from Iyo-Mishima station and then on foot. We have found no description of the path, the parking or the signage, and the newest photograph of it dates from 2010, so go prepared. In October and November its leaves turn pink and yellow and smell of burnt sugar as they fall. Both trees need a car. If you reach either, a dated photograph would help.

faq.q: Which tree in Shikokuchuo is a National Natural Monument?
faq.a: The Chinese juniper at Shimokashiwa, designated on 9 December 1924. The katsura on Mt Tamatori is a natural monument of Ehime Prefecture.

faq.q: How do you get to the katsura on Mt Tamatori?
faq.a: By car, roughly 25 kilometres of mountain road from Iyo-Mishima station, then on foot. We have found no published route description, so plan carefully.

faq.q: When is the best time to see the Tamatori katsura?
faq.a: October and November, when katsura leaves turn pink and yellow and give off a smell like burnt sugar as they fall.

sakurai.intro: In the Jionji district of Sakurai, a hollow zelkova leans out over the old road from a stone wall in front of the Amida Hall, beside Tamatsura Shrine. Locally it is known as the tree struck by lightning. The prefecture's sign says 800 years, the tourist association says 400, and its girth is about 6 metres. It stands in the open, free to see, and Sakurai is roughly half an hour by train from Nara.
sakurai.meta_description: The Amidaji zelkova in Sakurai, Nara: a hollow tree 6 metres round leaning over the old road, 400 or 800 years old by two accounts.
sakurai.question_answer: The Amidaji no Keyaki is a zelkova in front of the Amida Hall of Jionji in Sakurai, Nara Prefecture, beside Tamatsura Shrine. Its age is disputed: the prefecture's sign says 800 years, from tradition, and Sakurai's tourist association says 400. The Ministry of the Environment measured its girth at 6.05 metres in 2023. The trunk is hollow, and locally it is called the tree struck by lightning.
sakurai.question_meta: Sakurai's Amidaji zelkova: hollow, 6 metres round, 400 to 800 years old by two accounts, leaning over the old road at Jionji.
sakurai.question_context: Sakurai lies in the south-east of the Nara basin, roughly half an hour by train from Nara itself. The zelkova grows in the Jionji district, in front of the Amida Hall and beside Tamatsura Shrine, rising from a stone retaining wall and leaning over the old road below. It is out in the open and free to see. The sources do not agree on much. The prefecture's sign says 800 years, a figure from tradition; the city's tourist association says 400. Heights range from 10 metres in an older survey of the Kinki region to 22 metres in the Ministry of the Environment's giant-tree database of 2023, and girths from 5.2 metres to 6.05. What all of them describe is the same hollow old tree, known locally as the one struck by lightning. A survey of village giants photographed it in July 2023, so it was alive then. The nearest station named in the temple listings is Yamato-Asakura on the JR Sakurai Line, a walk from the hall. Our pin is approximate; the wall and the leaning trunk are the landmarks.

faq.q: How old is the zelkova at Amidaji in Sakurai?
faq.a: Between 400 and 800 years by the two accounts. The prefecture's sign says 800, from tradition; Sakurai's tourist association says 400.

faq.q: How do you get to the Amidaji zelkova?
faq.a: Take the JR Sakurai Line to Yamato-Asakura station and walk. Sakurai is roughly half an hour by train from Nara.

faq.q: Is it free to see?
faq.a: Yes. The tree stands in the open in front of the Amida Hall, beside Tamatsura Shrine.
